extracted.intended_audience: taxpayers, tax advisors, promoters, and tax practitioners involved in syndicated conservation easement transactions
extracted.subtask_description: Final Treasury/IRS regulations and explanatory preamble defining when syndicated conservation easement arrangements (and substantially similar transactions) are listed transactions that must be reported, including bright-line tests, methods for measuring investor investment, rebuttable presumptions, and scope rules (e.g., fee simple contributions, timing).

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuation of listing despite SECURE 2.0
rubrics_metrics.description: The Treasury Department and the IRS will continue to identify abusive syndicated conservation easement transactions as listed transactions notwithstanding the enactment of section 605 of the SECURE 2.0 Act (which added section 170(h)(7) and is prospective only).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Final regulations were modified after comments but retain listing authority to obtain reporting and identify promoters, material advisors, and donee organizations involved in abusive syndicated conservation easement transactions. The preamble explains that the regulations take a more "surgical approach" post-enactment but do not withdraw listing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three major classes of covered transactions
rubrics_metrics.description: These final regulations cover three major classes of abusive syndicated conservation easement transactions (and substantially similar transactions): (1) contributions occurring before December 30, 2022; (2) transactions for which a charitable contribution deduction is not automatically disallowed by section 170(h)(7); and (3) transactions that substitute the contribution of a fee simple interest in real property for the contribution of a conservation easement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each class is explicitly within the scope of the listed transaction rules; the regulations include provisions addressing timing, allocation, and property-interest substitutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: No duplicative reporting if previously disclosed under Notice 2017-10
rubrics_metrics.description: Taxpayers who fully disclosed their participation in syndicated conservation easement transactions pursuant to Notice 2017-10 do not need to disclose again under these final regulations for any taxable years covered by the prior disclosure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This prevents duplicative reporting where earlier disclosures already provided the targeted information to the IRS.

rubrics_metrics.name: No exception for transactions excluded from automatic disallowance under section 170(h)(7)
rubrics_metrics.description: The final regulations do not create exceptions for transactions that are excluded from the automatic disallowance rule in section 170(h)(7); Congress did not intend the statutory exceptions in 170(h)(7)(C)-(E) to limit the scope of listed transaction rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if a contribution is not automatically disallowed by 170(h)(7), it may still be abusive and a listed transaction if it meets the listed-transaction elements in these regulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transactions meeting statutory exceptions (C)-(E) can still be listed
rubrics_metrics.description: Transactions satisfying any of the three exceptions in section 170(h)(7)(C) through (E) that also contain all the elements of the listed transaction identified in these final regulations remain transactions the Treasury and IRS view as likely to be abusive and therefore listed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The presence of a statutory exception to automatic disallowance does not automatically exempt a transaction from being a listed transaction; assess all elements against the regulatory definition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allocation possibility of 2.5 times or more renders transaction a listed transaction for affected partners
rubrics_metrics.description: Any syndicated conservation easement transaction for which a charitable contribution deduction is not automatically disallowed because the partnership's contribution does not exceed 2.5 times the sum of partners' relevant basis is nevertheless a listed transaction with respect to any partner who received promotional materials offering the possibility of being allocated a share of the contribution that equals or exceeds 2.5 times that partner's investment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus is on what promotional materials offered to the partner (the possibility of an allocation ≥ 2.5x); that offer triggers reporting obligations as to that partner even if statutory disallowance does not apply at the partnership level.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contributions of fee simple or other real property interests treated as substantially similar
rubrics_metrics.description: A transaction that meets the elements of the listed transaction but consists of the contribution of a fee simple interest or a real property interest described in section 170(h)(2)(A) or (B) instead of a conservation easement is considered substantially similar to the syndicated conservation easement transaction identified in the regulations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This treatment relies on the broad definition of "substantially similar" in §1.6011-4(c)(4), congressional references, and the fact that fee simple/contribution-of-real-property transactions can result in similar tax consequences or be based on the same tax strategy. The final regulations explicitly state this and include an illustrative example.

rubrics_metrics.name: "Substantially similar" defined and construed broadly in favor of disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether a transaction is "substantially similar" depends on tax consequences, tax strategy, and other facts and circumstances; the regulatory definition in §1.6011-4(c)(4) is adopted and must be broadly construed in favor of disclosure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The rule serves as a backstop against attempts by advisors/promoters to avoid reporting. The regulations generally do not narrowly circumscribe what may be substantially similar, though they specify some exclusions (e.g., non-real property, non-pass-through entity contributions).

rubrics_metrics.name: 2.5 times threshold is a bright-line rule
rubrics_metrics.description: The 2.5 times threshold (a charitable contribution deduction equal to or exceeding 2.5 times the taxpayer's investment) is a bright-line rule: if promotional materials offer the possibility of allocation ≥ 2.5x, the transaction must be disclosed; transactions where both the offer and the actual allocation/deduction are less than 2.5x generally are not substantially similar.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The bright-line provides taxpayer certainty about reporting obligations. It does not create any safe harbor or imply that deductions under 2.5x are properly valued; valuation and substantiation rules (e.g., qualified appraisal per §1.170A-17) still apply and remain subject to IRS review. Also, if actual allocation ≥2.5x occurs contrary to promotional materials, a rebuttable presumption may apply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Highest suggested or implied deduction in promotional materials controls
rubrics_metrics.description: If promotional materials suggest or imply a range of possible charitable contribution deduction amounts, the highest suggested or implied deduction amount determines whether the 2.5 times rule is met; if one piece of promotional materials implies a higher amount than others, the highest amount controls.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This prevents promoters from creating inconsistent/ambiguous materials to circumvent the 2.5x bright line. Ambiguous language like promising an investment will "grow by" 2.5x without mentioning a charitable deduction can still trigger being substantially similar.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rebuttable presumption that 2.5x rule is met (three elements)
rubrics_metrics.description: A rebuttable presumption deems the 2.5x rule to be met if: (1) the pass-through entity donates a conservation easement within three years following a taxpayer's investment, (2) the pass-through entity allocates a charitable contribution deduction to the taxpayer equal to or exceeding 2.5 times the taxpayer's investment, and (3) the taxpayer claims a deduction equal to or exceeding 2.5 times the taxpayer's investment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The presumption may be rebutted if the taxpayer establishes to the satisfaction of the Commissioner that none of the promotional materials suggested or implied the possibility of an allocation ≥2.5x. The regulations decline to prescribe a specific method to rebut the presumption; rebuttal depends on facts and circumstances. Examples of possible rebuttal evidence include showing the partnership was not open to other investors or that property values increased materially after the investment. The Commissioner must respect taxpayer rights and rebuttal may be subject to judicial review; oral promotional materials are admissible insofar as they are evidence of what was stated, not for the truth of asserted matters (citing Fed. R. Evid. 801(c)(2)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Anti-stuffing method to determine taxpayer's investment
rubrics_metrics.description: For purposes of the 2.5x rule, the taxpayer's investment is limited to the portion of the taxpayer's investment that is attributable to the portion of the real property on which a conservation easement is placed and that produces the charitable contribution deduction (the "anti-stuffing method").
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an investor used non-cash assets to acquire the interest, the fair market value (not basis) of such assets is the relevant measure. Under §1.6011-9(d)(4)(ii), the amount is the portion of cash and fair market value of assets used to acquire the interest that is attributable to the real property giving rise to the charitable contribution deduction (or the portion thereof if an easement is on part of the property). The anti-stuffing method remains applicable for older contributions that predate relevant-basis rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relevant basis method for investments on/after Dec 30, 2022
rubrics_metrics.description: For contributions occurring on or after December 30, 2022, taxpayers may use their relevant basis, as determined under section 170(h)(7)(B) and the regulations thereunder, as the amount of their investment for purposes of the §1.6011-9(b)(1) 2.5x rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This alternative was added to mitigate duplicative calculations for partnerships and S corporations that must calculate relevant basis under section 170(h)(7). Using relevant basis is only permitted for contributions on or after Dec 30, 2022.

rubrics_metrics.name: Only anti-stuffing and relevant-basis methods permitted to determine investment
rubrics_metrics.description: Taxpayers may determine the amount of their investment in the pass-through entity only by one of the methods provided in §1.6011-9(d)(4) — the anti-stuffing method and, for contributions occurring on/after Dec 30, 2022, the relevant basis method. No other methods may be used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This restriction was adopted in response to comments requesting other definitions of "investment." The regulations therefore limit permissible methods to those specified to ensure consistency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Series of transactions to avoid the bright-line may be disregarded or recharacterized
rubrics_metrics.description: If a pass-through entity engages in a series of transactions (for example, contribution of an easement followed by contribution of a fee simple interest) with a principal purpose of avoiding the application of the bright-line 2.5x rule, the series may be disregarded, or the arrangement recharacterized in accordance with its substance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whether a series of transactions has the principal purpose of avoiding the bright-line rule is determined based on all facts and circumstances. This prevents artificial structuring to evade disclosure obligations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-real property contributions excluded from this listed-transaction definition
rubrics_metrics.description: Transactions involving contributions other than real property (for example, contributions of artwork or other personal property) are not considered "substantially similar" for purposes of these final regulations because the listed transaction relates to contributions of real property, not personal property.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Treasury and IRS may evaluate such transactions separately and could propose to identify them as listed transactions in future guidance, but they are excluded from this rule set.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transactions not involving a pass-through entity are excluded from being "substantially similar"
rubrics_metrics.description: Transactions that do not involve a contribution by a pass-through entity (such as contributions by an individual or a corporation) are not considered substantially similar transactions under these final regulations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such transactions could, however, be proposed to be identified as tax avoidance transactions in future guidance; exclusion here is specific to these regulations focused on pass-through entity–based syndications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transactions using other Code provisions may still be substantially similar
rubrics_metrics.description: A pass-through entity could use a deduction under a provision of the Code other than section 170 to obtain the same or a similar type of tax consequences (for example, section 642(c)), and such a transaction could be factually similar or based on the same or a similar tax strategy and therefore be substantially similar.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under §1.6011-4(f)(1), taxpayers uncertain whether a particular transaction is substantially similar may request a private letter ruling from the IRS.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 4965 carveout for qualified organizations retained
rubrics_metrics.description: To address concerns that the regulations could chill qualified organizations from accepting conservation easement contributions, these final regulations maintain the section 4965 carveout for qualified organizations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The retention of this carveout addresses commenters' concerns and is discussed further in Part V of the Summary of Comments and Explanation of Revisions.
